capitals.name: Nsachi (Aburi)
capitals.note: Capital placed at the centre of the core circle; the page gives no coordinates: 'In the mid-seventeenth century, the capital was moved to Nsachi, which was in the old Aburi state'; 'Until its destruction in 1730, Nyanaoase served as the imperial seat of government'. Asamankese is the place of origin.

capitals.name: Akwamufie
capitals.note: Approximate coordinates (the Akwamufie page gives none): 'A smaller state was formed at Akwamufie in the early 1730s' (Akwamu page); ceremonial capital today.

region.text: the Akwamu state round Asamankese, Nsachi and Nyanaoase

ledger.note: c. 1629: the Akwamu state is first on record. 'The Akwamu Empire was an Akan state that rose in the 17th century'; 'The earliest reference to Akwamu appears on a Dutch Map of the Gold Coast dated to 1629'; the infobox gives '16th century' for the start. The founding year is not on the page; 1629 is the first dated reference.
1677: Ansa Sasraku I attacks the Ga of Accra. 'In 1677, Akwamuhene Nana Ansa Sasraku I launched a major attack against the Ga kingdom of Accra.'

region.text: the Adangme-speaking kingdom of Ladoku (Ningo and the coast east of Accra)

ledger.note: 1679: Ladoku falls. 'in 1679, its armies overran the Adangme-speaking kingdom of Ladoku', Ningo among the centres taken.

region.text: Great Accra, Small Accra, Osu and Labadi

ledger.note: 1681: the last Ga towns fall. 'Between 1680 and 1681, the remaining Ga towns, Small Accra, Osu, and Labadi, were defeated. For the next fifty years, Accra remained a province of Akwamu.' A mutiny at Christiansborg led by Pieter Bolt took place in 1680.
1681: the Ga war ends in Akwamu's victory; Accra a province for fifty years.

1693: Akwamu seizes Christiansborg. 'In 1693, under Basua's direction, Akwamu forces seized Christiansborg Castle from the Danes.' The Danish Gold Coast dossier carries the mirror loss (1693) and the Danish return (1694); this page is silent on how the castle was given back.

region.text: Christiansborg Castle (Osu), back in Danish hands after about a year

ledger.note: 1694: the Danes recover Christiansborg. 'The fort was held by Akwamu for about a year, during which trade continued under the Danish flag' (Akwamu page); the year is 1693 plus that year, matching the Danish Gold Coast dossier's 1694 gain. Reviewer af-04-x (2026-10-19): added as the mirror of danish-gold-coast 1694.

region.text: Little Popo and the coast from the Volta to Little Popo

ledger.note: 1702 (April): Akwamu takes Little Popo. 'In early 1702, an initial invasion across the Volta River was repelled'; 'Little Popo was captured in April'.

1702 (May): Whydah falls to Akwamu and pays tribute. 'followed by the seizure of Whydah in May'; 'Though Whydah was eventually destroyed by Dahomey in the 1720s, it remained tributary to Akwamu for over two decades.'
1727 (26 February): Dahomey takes Whydah. The Akwamu page says only 'destroyed by Dahomey in the 1720s'; the Agaja page: 'On February 26, 1727, Agaja attacked Whydah and burned the palace.'

region.text: the western territories: the core, Accra, the Ladoku coast and the Popo coast

ledger.note: 1730: the Akyem coalition destroys Nyanaoase and takes the western lands. 'In 1730 a coalition of forces from the northwest and west destroyed Nyanaoase'; 'Akwamu lost its western territories following the 1730-31 invasion by Akyem.' Accra and the Ladoku coast are the researcher's reading of 'western territories'. wars.name: Akwamu-Ga war

zones.text: Accra, Small Accra, Osu and Labadi

wars.outcome: Akwamu victory: Ladoku overrun in 1679, the remaining Ga towns defeated 1680-81; Accra a province of Akwamu for fifty years.
wars.note: The page gives no battle dates for 1677-1678.

wars.name: Akwamu campaign against Agona
wars.outcome: 'In 1689, Ansa Sasraku led his final major military campaign against the kingdom of Agona'; the page gives no result or land.

wars.name: Akwamu seizure of Christiansborg
wars.outcome: Akwamu forces seized Christiansborg Castle from the Danes in 1693; the page gives no end (the Danish dossier has the Danes back in 1694).

wars.name: Akwamu conquest of Little Popo and Whydah
wars.outcome: A first invasion across the Volta was repelled in early 1702; Little Popo was captured in April and Whydah seized in May; Whydah stayed tributary for over two decades.

wars.name: Akyem invasion of Akwamu
wars.outcome: Akyem and allies destroyed Nyanaoase in 1730 and Akwamu lost its western territories in the 1730-31 invasion; a smaller state formed at Akwamufie in the early 1730s.

certainty.note: No page gives a frontier; the shapes are circles and regions standing for named towns and peoples. The coast (Accra, Little Popo) is firmer than the forest interior.

notes: Akwamu has no Cliopatria row. Three pages opened (Nyanaoase did not exist as a page: URL_NOT_FOUND). The Akwamu page gives no founding year ('rose in the 17th century'; infobox '16th century'), so 1629 (earliest dated reference) is the start at confidence 1; no area figure, so no infobox check; the 400 km coast length is the only extent. The Ashanti dossier (af-04-a) uses denkyira and akwamu as counterparts: Osei Tutu sought refuge at the Akwamu court (page) but the page does not say Denkyira was Akwamu's overlord or when. The Danish dossier has loss 1693 / gain 1694 against akwamu; this page only has the 1693 seizure. Disagreement: Accra 'a province' for fifty years (to about 1730) vs the Ashanti dossier's 1742 Accra occupation. Not placed: Akwapim, Fante, Agona and the Volta crossing beyond the Lomé circle; the 1742 Ashanti conquest of Accra. The 1731-1886 rump is a 25 km circle round Akwamufie with no page for its extent. Counterparts without dossier: Ga kingdom of Accra, Ladoku, Akyem (coalition), kingdom-of-whydah (planned), danish-gold-coast (exists). Gazetteer names needed: Akwamufie (Eastern Region, Ghana, about 6.3N 0.08E).
